mobileAccess.title: Mobile Access
mobileAccess.subtitle: Open Vibisual in your phone's browser over the same Wi-Fi. Turn it on, open the address below on your phone, then enter the pairing code.
mobileAccess.noNetwork: No local network address detected — check your Wi-Fi or network adapter.
mobileAccess.pairingHint: Your phone asks for this code the first time it connects. Paired devices stay connected.
mobileAccess.locked: Too many failed attempts — pairing is locked. Generate a new code to unlock.
mobileAccess.securityNote: Anyone on your network with this code can control Vibisual and run agents on this PC. Keep it on trusted Wi-Fi only.
mobileAccess.externalSubtitle: Reach this PC over the internet. Vibisual asks your router to open a port automatically (UPnP) and serves over encrypted HTTPS.
mobileAccess.externalMapping: Asking your router to open a port…
mobileAccess.externalCgnat: Your internet connection doesn't have a public address (carrier-grade NAT), so a port can't be opened from here. Use a VPN such as Tailscale, or ask your ISP for a public IP.
mobileAccess.externalManual: Couldn't open a port automatically (your router's UPnP may be off). To do it manually, forward external TCP port {{port}} to {{ip}}:{{port}} on this PC in your router settings.
mobileAccess.externalManualUrl: Once the port is forwarded, connect from outside at this address:
mobileAccess.externalHttpsNote: Uses a self-signed certificate — your phone shows a security warning the first time. Tap "Advanced → proceed" to continue; the connection is still encrypted.
mobileAccess.qrSubtitle: Scan with your phone's camera — Vibisual opens and pairs itself, no address or code to type. Each QR works for {{minutes}} minutes.

guide.title: Guide
guide.subtitle: A tour of what Vibisual can do — and an inventory of features built so far.

start.intro: Vibisual visualizes what your AI agents are doing, in real time, as a bubble map.
start.openFolderD: File → Open Folder to start tracking a project. Each project opens in its own tab.
start.watchD: When Claude Code runs, the files and folders it touches appear as bubbles and pulse as they change.
start.optionsD: File → Options to choose the default model, tools, permission mode and Claude Code binary for new agents.

bubbleMap.intro: The canvas draws your project as bubbles linked by hierarchy and activity.
bubbleMap.typesD: Files, folders, agents, Bash, edits, iframes and more — each color-coded by category.
bubbleMap.sizeD: Bigger bubbles were touched more often. A pulsing bubble is active right now.
bubbleMap.contextD: An agent bubble fills like water to show how much of its context window is in use.
bubbleMap.ghostD: Deleted or renamed nodes linger as faded ghosts so the trail isn't lost.

agents.intro: Beyond passive tracking, you can create and orchestrate your own agents from the canvas.
agents.customD: Right-click the canvas to spawn your own agent bubble and give it a command.
agents.autoD: Describe what you want in plain language; a builder agent designs and wires up a whole team for you.
agents.configD: Click a bubble to set its model, tools, permission mode, effort, isolation and color.
agents.pipelineD: Run independent sessions and chain agents together with pipeline, teams or hybrid strategies.

taskEdges.intro: Connect two custom agents with a Task Edge to delegate work between them.
taskEdges.drawD: Drag from one custom-agent bubble to another to create a delegation edge between them.
taskEdges.kindsD: Command, artifact, request or critique — the kind says what flows across the edge.
taskEdges.critiqueD: A critique edge can force the target agent to rework its output until a reviewer accepts it.

ide.intro: Double-click an agent to open the IDE overlay — its live output, sessions and reports.
ide.streamD: Follow the agent's messages, tool calls and results as they happen.
ide.cardsD: Finished work and things you need to do yourself are split into color-coded cards.
ide.reviewD: When an agent finishes a fix, a purple card shows what changed and what to check.
ide.dockD: Drag the overlay's title bar to float it, or snap it to the right as a side panel.

navigation.panD: Drag the canvas to pan and scroll to zoom; the minimap shows where you are.
navigation.tabsD: Each open folder is a tab; drag a tab out of the bar to pop it into its own window.
navigation.inspectorD: Hold Alt to highlight elements and click to copy; Shift-drag to select a region.
navigation.copyD: Select custom agents and edges, then Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V to clone them into another project.

history.intro: Vibisual remembers your projects between runs.
history.saveD: The whole graph is checkpointed to disk and restored the next time you open Vibisual.
history.replayD: Scrub a timeline to replay how the map grew over a session.

shortcuts.intro: Keyboard shortcuts speed up navigation and editing. They pause while you type in an input or terminal.
shortcuts.bookmarkD: Alt+1…0 pins a bubble or session to a slot; press 1…0 to jump back to it.
shortcuts.copyD: Ctrl+C / Ctrl+V (Cmd on macOS) copies and pastes selected agents, edges and comment boxes.
shortcuts.inspectorD: Hold Alt to inspect and click to copy an element; Shift-drag for region select.
shortcuts.closeD: Esc closes menus, popups and the IDE overlay.

autoAgent.buildingHint: The builder is designing agents and connections on the canvas. Open this bubble to watch it work.

plugins.title: Plugins
plugins.unsupported: Not supported in this version yet.
plugins.offNote: Turning a plugin off only hides its contributions — nothing it created is deleted, and everything comes back when you turn it on again.

lethalTrifecta.heading: Lethal Trifecta
lethalTrifecta.prescription: Outbound communication is the cheapest leg to cut — add WebFetch (and Bash, if this agent can work without it) to Disallowed Tools in Agent Settings.
lethalTrifecta.alreadyCut: One leg is already cut, so an injection cannot turn into a leak on this agent.
lethalTrifecta.isolatedNote: Working in an isolated worktree — that narrows the damage, but it does not cut a leg.
lethalTrifecta.displayOnly: Display only — this section never changes permissions.

title.critical: Lethal trifecta: all three legs open, with no approval prompt

lethalTrifecta.desc: Shows on every agent bubble how many of the three legs an attack needs — sensitive data access, untrusted content, outbound communication — that agent currently holds. Cutting one leg breaks the path. Display only: it never changes permissions.

leastPrivilege.desc: Splits the tools granted to an agent by what they can actually do — irreversible changes, reach to the outside, read-only — so over-granting is visible. Judged from the tool list alone.
leastPrivilege.heading: Least Privilege

badge.wide: {{count}} powerful tools — consider taking some back

leastPrivilege.lockedNote: {{tools}} cannot be removed from the UI — the delegation path depends on it. Use Disallowed Tools instead if this agent must not have it.
leastPrivilege.displayOnly: Display only — this section never changes settings.

blastRadius.desc: Lists what this agent could reach, change and send if it were fully taken over — that list is the blast radius. An isolated worktree narrows it by one step.
blastRadius.heading: Blast Radius
blastRadius.isolatedNote: Isolated worktree — damage stays in the copy, so the radius counts one step smaller.
blastRadius.narrowHint: Read-only by default, writes to named paths only, network to an allowed list — that is how a radius shrinks.

autonomyLevel.desc: Shows which rung this agent sits on — propose only, run after approval, or run on its own and report. Leaving autonomy as all-or-nothing is the most common design failure.
autonomyLevel.heading: Autonomy Level
autonomyLevel.timeoutHint: Stepping away turns approval into automatic consent — the rung effectively moves up.
autonomyLevel.ladderNote: Autonomy is something you raise as trust accumulates, not something granted from the start.

levelDesc.approve: Mutating tools raise an approval prompt.
levelDesc.autonomous: No approval prompt appears at all.

longHorizon.desc: Tracks how long a session has been running — turns, elapsed time, and the last to-do progress. Long tasks usually fail from exhausted context and accumulated error, not from lack of ability.
longHorizon.heading: Long-Horizon Task
longHorizon.shortNote: Still short — nothing to watch yet.
longHorizon.longNote: Write down decisions and file paths before compaction runs — summaries drop the specifics first.

rogueAgent.desc: Shows how long an agent has been silent while its sessions are still alive. Most incidents start with “I did not know that was still running”, not with malice.
rogueAgent.heading: Idle & Rogue

badge.idle: Quiet for {{elapsed}} with sessions still alive

rogueAgent.idleNote: Design the moment you turn an agent off, not just the moment you create one.

guardrails.desc: Shows whether anything actually stops a tool call. A guardrail placed right before the tool call catches damage at the last moment; placed only in front of the model, it catches too late.
guardrails.heading: Guardrails
guardrails.notePlacement: The approval prompt sits right before the tool call — the position that catches damage latest and cheapest.
guardrails.noteNone: No approval prompt appears, so nothing intercepts a tool call before it runs.

humanInTheLoop.desc: Checks whether a human confirmation stands in front of irreversible actions. Approving everything makes approval meaningless; approving nothing causes incidents. The test is reversibility.
humanInTheLoop.heading: Human in the Loop
humanInTheLoop.note: Better than adding approvals is making actions undoable — trash instead of delete, versions instead of overwrite, draft instead of send.

allowlist.desc: Shows how close this agent is to “only these are allowed”. A blocklist leaks through whatever you forgot; an allowlist fails toward safety as time passes.
allowlist.heading: Allowlist
allowlist.note: The highest-value place to apply an allowlist is network destinations — that alone narrows the last leg of a leak.

sandboxing.desc: Shows whether the agent runs on an isolated copy. Filesystem isolation alone is not enough — without network isolation the last leg of a leak stays open.
sandboxing.heading: Sandboxing
sandboxing.note: Vibisual isolates the filesystem through git worktree. Network is not isolated, so outbound paths stay open even in a worktree.

nonHumanIdentity.desc: Asks the practical question: can you cut off this one agent right now? If the answer is “I would have to stop everything”, there is no identity design.
nonHumanIdentity.heading: Non-Human Identity
nonHumanIdentity.noteOwned: We created this agent, so it carries its own settings and can be stopped on its own.
nonHumanIdentity.noteExternal: This session was registered through hooks and belongs to Claude Code — we have no handle that stops it alone.

containment.desc: Assumes the attack succeeds and asks what is still possible. Success comes not from the most aggressive filter but from a structurally limited radius when something does get through.
containment.heading: Containment
containment.note: Ask “what is possible once it is through”, not “how do I block it”. If you cannot answer the first, the design is not finished.

auditTrail.desc: Counts what is left of this agent’s trace — turns recorded and session IDs preserved — so that “who did this” can still be answered afterwards.
auditTrail.heading: Audit Trail
auditTrail.note: Keeping the original run log, stamping decisions with their source session, and marking commits with the agent as co-author is the minimum set.

contextRot.desc: Shows how full the context window is. The window size is a ceiling, not a target — quality often drops noticeably near half, and similar-looking distractors hurt more than length alone.
contextRot.heading: Context Rot
contextRot.noteLow: Plenty of room. Measure your own effective window with real work rather than trusting the advertised size.
contextRot.noteHigh: Write decisions and file paths out to a file before compaction runs — summaries drop the specifics first.

costPerTask.desc: Looks at cost per completed task rather than per token, and shows tokens per turn — background work that produces little can quietly take most of the bill.
costPerTask.heading: Cost per Task
costPerTask.note: The estimate counts input and output only; cache tokens are not accumulated per session, so the real figure is somewhat higher.

modelRouting.desc: Puts the current model next to the size of the work so promotion or demotion is a visible decision. It never switches models for you — that stays your call.
modelRouting.heading: Model Routing

advice.fit: Model and workload look matched. Cascades pay off when the cheap model handles the easy majority.
advice.upgrade: This has become a long task on a small model. Promoting it usually costs less than repeated retries.
advice.downgrade: A short task on the largest model. A cheaper model would likely finish this identically.

reasoningEffort.desc: Shows thinking effort next to the size of the work. More thinking is not always better — there is a measured range where extra deliberation lowers accuracy on simple, factual tasks.
reasoningEffort.heading: Reasoning Effort
reasoningEffort.noteMeasure: Raise effort and measure, rather than leaving the maximum on — turning it up costs tokens on every turn.
reasoningEffort.noteOverthinking: Maximum thinking on a very short task. This is the range where cost rises and accuracy can fall.

toolUse.desc: Shows how much of the context window the tool definitions alone take. Past a few dozen tools the definitions cost tens of thousands of tokens and selection accuracy drops with them.
toolUse.heading: Tool Use
toolUse.note: Removing tools this agent never uses improves cost and selection accuracy at the same time.

tokenBudget.desc: Splits the context window into fixed sections first. Without a per-section budget, one section quietly pushes the others out — that is how instructions get truncated on a heavy day.
tokenBudget.heading: Token Budget
tokenBudget.note: Characters divided by four approximates tokens. Fix the ceilings as constants and state what gets cut when they overflow.

systemPrompt.desc: Shows the size of the always-on instruction layer. A system prompt has to sit at the right altitude — too specific and it is brittle, too abstract and it is ignored.
systemPrompt.heading: System Prompt
systemPrompt.note: Background work such as summarising or classifying rarely needs a general-purpose prompt — a short dedicated one with no tools is usually the right answer.
systemPrompt.noteLong: These rules ride along on every single turn. Long rules cost tokens continuously and get diluted first when the session grows.

subagent.desc: Shows whether context isolation is actually happening. The point of a subagent is not speed but keeping exploration notes and verbose tool output out of the main thread.
subagent.heading: Subagent Isolation
subagent.note: Isolation buys a clean context but creates a new bottleneck — handoff quality. The main thread should see results, not the search.

fanOut.desc: Counts how many branches run at once. Parallelism pays only when the subtasks are genuinely independent; otherwise it produces duplicated work and contradictory conclusions.
fanOut.heading: Fan-out
fanOut.note: Decide how results will be merged before splitting. Without a merge rule the integration step becomes the bottleneck.
fanOut.noteWide: Many branches at once. Ask whether these are truly independent — if they need each other’s results, sequencing is cheaper.

orchestrator.desc: Shows whether this agent acts as a supervisor or does the work itself. Gathering agents without a supervisor is a known anti-pattern — scale grows and reliability drops.
orchestrator.heading: Orchestrator
orchestrator.note: The recommended shape is a supervisor that judges while the actual tool execution lives below it.

planAndExecute.desc: Shows whether a plan exists and how far it has progressed. Writing the plan to a file means it survives compaction, which is the main reason to keep one.
planAndExecute.heading: Plan and Execute
planAndExecute.note: A plan the user can approve and edit is worth more than a faster start.
planAndExecute.noteNoPlan: No plan recorded yet. For work with many ordered steps, a written plan is what keeps the thread from losing its way.

reactPattern.desc: Reason and act alternating is the default shape, not one option among many. This card watches for the signal that it is no longer enough — a long run with nothing written down.
reactPattern.heading: ReAct
reactPattern.note: The signals that ReAct alone is not enough: circling the same tool, losing the goal, moving on without verifying.
reactPattern.noteDrifting: A long run with no plan recorded. This is where a written plan or a verifier step usually pays for itself.

scopeCreep.desc: Watches the to-do list for growth and for quiet shrinkage. In AI collaboration the shrinking direction matters just as much — the user believes it was all done and finds out late.
scopeCreep.heading: Scope
scopeCreep.note: Scope is the instructing side’s decision, not the model’s discretion.
scopeCreep.noteGrew: The list grew well past where it started. Worth checking whether that growth was agreed.
scopeCreep.noteShrank: The list shrank from its peak. Confirm those items were finished rather than dropped.

reviewGate.desc: Counts whether completion was handed over in a reviewable shape. Long prose reports do not get read; a change list plus check points does.
reviewGate.heading: Review Gate
reviewGate.note: What makes review cheap is separating “what changed” from “what to verify”.

structuredOutput.desc: Shows whether this agent reports through a schema rather than prose. Once one agent’s output becomes another’s input, a parse failure is a pipeline stop.
structuredOutput.heading: Structured Output
structuredOutput.note: Handoff packets, scoring results and tool arguments are all better received as schemas than as sentences.

instructionDrift.desc: Early instructions lose their grip as a session grows, and compaction dilutes them faster. “I said it once” does not hold.
instructionDrift.heading: Instruction Drift
instructionDrift.note: Important constraints need re-injecting each turn, or marking as a preserved section through compaction.
instructionDrift.noteLong: This session is long enough that early instructions have likely faded. Re-state the constraints that still matter.

semanticMemory.desc: Counts how many facts are actually settled. What matters is not how many cards were stored but how many slots hold a single current truth; slots whose value split are waiting on a human.
semanticMemory.heading: Semantic Memory
semanticMemory.note: Scale decides storage: a few hundred entries belong in files, hundreds of thousands in a vector store. Choosing infrastructure before measuring scale is the common over-design.

memoryInvalidation.desc: Missing memory makes a model say it does not know; stale memory makes it confidently wrong. Marking rather than deleting lets the next person judge.
memoryInvalidation.heading: Memory Invalidation
memoryInvalidation.note: In code, a change to the linked file is the most accurate staleness signal — path matching leaves almost no false positives.
memoryInvalidation.notePending: Some cards were flagged because their linked files changed. Compare them with the current code and confirm or retire them.

forgettingPolicy.desc: Storage policy is easier than forgetting policy. Memory that only grows loses retrieval precision until it is worse than having none.
forgettingPolicy.heading: Forgetting Policy
forgettingPolicy.note: The safe shape is a total budget with overflow moved to archive rather than deleted — automatic permanent deletion leaves no way back.

supersede.desc: When new knowledge conflicts with old, closing beats deleting. Two timestamps — opened and closed — give an immutable record and a clean present at once.
supersede.heading: Supersede
supersede.note: Contradiction is not similarity alone — negation matters, so that “use A” and “never use A” are recognised as the same subject.

memoryDrift.desc: Repeatedly rewriting a memory polishes it away from the original until invented detail hardens into fact. The defence is to keep entries immutable.
memoryDrift.heading: Memory Drift
memoryDrift.note: Updates are a new entry plus closing the old one. There is no path where the model rewrites an existing body.

memoryConsolidation.desc: Distilling episodes into facts is not free — it is a lossy operation. Keep the original and add the distillation rather than replacing it.
memoryConsolidation.heading: Memory Consolidation
memoryConsolidation.note: Two traps: naive summarisation loses encoded facts, and weak deduplication lets new records overwrite old ones that were still true.

episodicMemory.desc: The raw experience is first-class evidence. Keep only summaries and there is no way left to verify them or undo their errors.
episodicMemory.heading: Episodic Memory
episodicMemory.note: Extracted knowledge should carry its source session and timestamp so it can be walked back to the original.

proceduralMemory.desc: Of the three memory layers this is the one where files are clearly the right answer — a procedure is needed whole when the task comes up, not retrieved piecemeal.
proceduralMemory.heading: Procedural Memory
proceduralMemory.note: Skill files and agent definitions are the physical form of procedural memory, and version control is their decisive advantage over a vector store.

workingMemory.desc: Fast, and gone when the session ends. This alone never becomes a system that gets smarter with use — but trying to promote everything to long-term memory fails just as surely.
workingMemory.heading: Working Memory
workingMemory.note: Most of a conversation should be consumed and discarded. Deciding what gets promoted is the first step of memory design.

memoryTool.desc: Separates memory that was pushed in at spawn from memory the agent went and looked up. Notes in files survive compaction, which is what makes this the lightest form of lasting memory.
memoryTool.heading: Memory Tool
memoryTool.note: Try file-based notes before standing up separate vector infrastructure — the overhead is close to none.

progressiveDisclosure.desc: Rather than loading everything up front, hand over an index and let the body be fetched when it matters. This card watches whether the same bundle keeps getting re-injected instead.
progressiveDisclosure.heading: Progressive Disclosure
progressiveDisclosure.note: Pasting whole documents is manufacturing context rot on purpose. “If the task is X, read file Y” is the same idea done cheaply.

contextPollution.desc: Rot is about length; pollution is about mixing. Failed attempts, abandoned approaches and verbose tool output linger — and a wrong intermediate conclusion keeps being treated as fact.
contextPollution.heading: Context Pollution
contextPollution.note: This is the real reason to use subagents — not speed, but letting each subtask start from a clean context.
contextPollution.noteMixed: Many turns are piling into few sessions. Splitting the next subtask into its own session keeps the wrong middles from following along.

agentHarness.desc: Gathers everything wrapped around the model — tools, permission, isolation, skills, rules. The same model produces very different results depending on this layer, which is where the competition moved.
agentHarness.heading: Agent Harness
agentHarness.note: Benchmark numbers carry scaffold inflation — the same model scores differently under a different harness, so compare harnesses, not just models.

scaffold.desc: Shows how much glue is written around the model — rules, skills, turn caps. Gains on long-running agents come from better scaffolding far more than from a smarter model.
scaffold.heading: Scaffold
scaffold.note: Papers say “scaffold”, products say “harness”. Same thing, different nuance — one is code structure, the other is operations.

agentLoop.desc: Shows the rhythm of the loop and whether it has a stopping condition. A loop that cannot stop itself makes turn caps and kill switches safety devices rather than conveniences.
agentLoop.heading: Agent Loop
agentLoop.note: Measuring cost and time per loop iteration is where operating an agent starts.
agentLoop.noteUncapped: No turn cap is set. Without one, the only thing that stops a loop is you noticing it.

handoffPacket.desc: Counts how work is handed over. The real bottleneck in multi-agent setups is handoff quality, not model strength — hand over as free prose and it leaks every time.
handoffPacket.heading: Handoff
handoffPacket.note: Fix the packet shape — goal, what was tried, constraints, where the output is, and what could not be confirmed.

verifierCritic.desc: Checks whether the writer and the checker are separate. A critic that shares the writer’s blind spots simply stamps bad answers as good.
verifierCritic.heading: Verifier and Critic
verifierCritic.note: Executable verification — tests, lint, typecheck — is cheaper and more accurate than a critic, so put it first.
verifierCritic.noteSelf: No critique edge. Reviewing one’s own output usually ends in a formal pass; a separate critic or an executable check is what catches things.

hookLifecycle.desc: Hooks arrive more often than people expect — believing a “session end” hook fires once when it fires every turn is a classic cause of runaway behaviour.
hookLifecycle.heading: Hook Lifecycle
hookLifecycle.note: Synchronous I/O inside a hook stalls the agent for exactly that long. Queue and coalesce instead.

contextWindow.desc: The window is a ceiling, not a target. “This model has 200k so 150k is fine” does not follow — measure your own effective window with real work.
contextWindow.heading: Context Window
contextWindow.note: Do not trust needle-in-a-haystack scores — they measure lexical lookup, not the difficulty of real long-context work.

testTimeCompute.desc: Buying thinking time instead of a bigger model pays off over a wide range. In practice it means quality, latency and cost became a dial you can turn per task.
testTimeCompute.heading: Test-Time Compute
testTimeCompute.note: Turning the dial up on easy work is pure waste. Match the amount of thinking to the difficulty of the task.

extendedThinking.desc: Long deliberation before answering helps with planning, debugging and multi-step reasoning — but thinking tokens also occupy the window and get billed.
extendedThinking.heading: Extended Thinking
extendedThinking.note: Whether to show the thinking to the user is a product decision — it builds trust, but wrong intermediate guesses read like settled conclusions.
extendedThinking.noteOn: Deep thinking is on and the window is filling. In long sessions, clearing old thinking blocks becomes necessary rather than optional.

reflexion.desc: Self-critique works when it rests on an executable signal such as a failing test. Reflection without evidence is plausible noise.
reflexion.heading: Reflexion
reflexion.note: This pattern works best in coding, where tests act as an objective judge. Where no such judge exists, its value drops sharply.

contextEngineering.desc: Counts how many of the context patterns this agent actually uses — index over injection, tool trimming, active retrieval, thinking control.
contextEngineering.heading: Context Engineering
contextEngineering.note: The question moved from “how do I word the prompt” to “what do I show it”.

agentSkills.desc: Skills give procedural knowledge as files rather than prompt text. Names and descriptions load at start, bodies only when relevant — so dozens of skills barely raise the standing cost.
agentSkills.heading: Agent Skills
agentSkills.note: Reusable procedures — deployment steps, review checklists, internal API usage — belong in files under version control, not in a prompt.

trajectoryEval.desc: Scores how the answer was reached rather than the answer itself. The same result after 3 tool calls and after 40 are entirely different systems, and outcome-only evaluation cannot see that difference.
trajectoryEval.heading: Trajectory Eval
trajectoryEval.note: Looking at the order of tool calls catches wasteful or risky patterns before they reach production.

eval.desc: Agents are non-deterministic, so a single run is not evidence — the same input has to be looked at as a distribution. This counts how often an instruction was actually repeated.
eval.heading: Eval
eval.note: Whatever can be checked deterministically — format, schema, required fields, forbidden words — is cheaper and more accurate in code than through a judge model.

goldenSet.desc: Representativeness matters more than size, and real past failures have to be in there. A set built only from successes always scores full marks.
goldenSet.heading: Golden Set
goldenSet.note: Adding a failure to the set the moment it is found is the cheapest quality infrastructure there is — one incident becomes one permanent regression test.

regressionSuite.desc: Agents often undo an earlier fix because the reason for it is not in their context. A regression test stands in for that memory — documents may go unread, a failing test cannot.
regressionSuite.heading: Regression Suite
regressionSuite.note: The subtler the fix, the more it needs a test. “Change this and that breaks” survives far better as a test than as a comment.

traceSpan.desc: A trace is the whole path of one request and spans are its segments. Model calls, tool runs and judgements all become spans.
traceSpan.heading: Trace and Span
traceSpan.note: Carry tokens and cost on the spans and observability doubles as cost analysis.

observability.desc: Being able to reconstruct “why did it do that” afterwards is what makes a non-deterministic system fixable. A bug you cannot reproduce cannot be fixed without records.
observability.heading: Observability
observability.note: Observation can kill the app — a synchronous disk write on every tool event becomes the bottleneck itself. Sampling, debounce and batching are the basic devices.

llmAsJudge.desc: A strong model scoring output is a practical compromise where no correct string exists. It has known biases — it prefers longer answers, favours its own family, and is swayed by presentation order.
llmAsJudge.heading: LLM as Judge
llmAsJudge.note: Without checking the judge against human scoring, there is no way to know the judge itself is wrong.

evalDrivenDevelopment.desc: Build the evaluation first and fix towards its score. The decisive step was joining evaluation and guardrails — the offline judge gets promoted into the runtime gate.
evalDrivenDevelopment.heading: Eval-Driven Development
evalDrivenDevelopment.note: Changing a prompt with no evaluation behind it is the unlicensed driving of this field.

hallucinationGuard.desc: In agents the usual form is inventing an API, file or function that does not exist. Typecheck, lint and tests catch invented APIs immediately — far more reliably than asking the model to double-check.
hallucinationGuard.heading: Hallucination Guard
hallucinationGuard.note: Stale documents produce confidently wrong answers that retrieval cannot fix — search will faithfully fetch the wrong thing.

worktreeIsolation.desc: Once several agents run at once this becomes required infrastructure — branches alone cannot be checked out twice, and two agents in one directory overwrite each other.
worktreeIsolation.heading: Worktree Isolation
worktreeIsolation.note: Isolating is the easy half. Dependencies have to be installed per tree, conflicts pile up at merge time, and integration design is the harder part.
worktreeIsolation.noteIsolated: Work is happening on a separate tree, so a merge is still ahead. That is where the conflicts arrive all at once.

vibeCoding.desc: Its defining trait is accepting output without reading every line. It has not disappeared — its range narrowed to prototypes, exploration and throwaway tools.
vibeCoding.heading: Vibe Coding
vibeCoding.note: The judgement is simply how long this code has to live — a day means vibe, three years means specification.

agenticEngineering.desc: The difference between “coding with AI” and “operating agents” sits here. Programming through agents became the expert default — but with more supervision and review attached.
agenticEngineering.heading: Agentic Engineering
agenticEngineering.note: Rule documents, evaluation sets, loss-prevention infrastructure and commit gates are all spending done in advance — a fraction of what a later rescue costs.

rag.desc: Shows what evidence was actually pulled in for this agent. In Vibisual that channel is Project Brain, so the card counts the cards that arrived rather than guessing at retrieval quality.
rag.heading: RAG
rag.note: Retrieval cannot fix a confidently wrong source — it will faithfully fetch the wrong thing.

agenticRag.desc: Separates memory pushed in at spawn from memory the agent went and looked for. Push-only means the same bundle rides along every time; active search means it arrives when it is needed.
agenticRag.heading: Agentic RAG
agenticRag.note: A fixed pipeline retrieves once; an agent decides when it needs more and goes back.

grounding.desc: Checks whether claims are tied to something verifiable — the ability to read the source, and evidence that actually arrived.
grounding.heading: Grounding
grounding.note: Reading the file beats being told about the file. Grounding is what makes a claim checkable rather than plausible.

agenticFileSearch.desc: In a codebase, walking the filesystem usually beats building an index — indexes go stale, grep always sees the current state.
agenticFileSearch.heading: Agentic File Search
agenticFileSearch.note: Letting the agent explore — estimating complexity from file size, purpose from names — is the same idea as progressive disclosure.

vectorDb.desc: Scale decides storage. A few hundred entries belong in files with text search; hundreds of thousands justify a vector store. Choosing infrastructure before measuring scale is the common over-design.
vectorDb.heading: Vector DB
vectorDb.note: Vibisual keeps memory in files on purpose. This card exists to notice the day that choice stops paying off.

gracefulDegradation.desc: A guardrail has to fail safe — when judgement fails, the answer is block, not pass. Here the fork is what happens when an approval prompt goes unanswered.
gracefulDegradation.heading: Graceful Degradation
gracefulDegradation.note: Fail-open is a legitimate choice when work must not stall — but it should be a choice, not a default nobody noticed.
gracefulDegradation.noteOpen: If you step away, unanswered prompts turn into approvals. Switch to auto-block for work where that would matter.

idempotency.desc: Agents paper over failures with retries. A tool that is not idempotent doubles the data on one retry, which is why this is treated as a base requirement rather than a best practice.
idempotency.heading: Idempotency
idempotency.note: For tools that cannot be undone, an idempotency key in the schema is what makes a retry safe.

separationOfConcerns.desc: When an agent edits one place, the blast radius of side effects is the size of the incident. Kept separate, a wrong edit ends inside its own boundary.
separationOfConcerns.heading: Separation of Concerns
separationOfConcerns.note: The agent version of this principle is context-centric decomposition — the agent that owns a feature also owns its tests.

eventDriven.desc: Vibisual itself runs on hook events, so this card shows how much signal actually flowed through this agent and where it came from.
eventDriven.heading: Event-Driven
eventDriven.note: Loose coupling and independent failure are the point — but they also mean nothing tells you an event was dropped.

backpressure.desc: When arrival outpaces processing the queue grows, and left alone the overflow is either silently dropped or brings everything to a stop.
backpressure.heading: Backpressure
backpressure.note: Many branches at once is not throughput if they contend for the same context and the same review attention.

durableExecution.desc: Long tasks fail from crashes in the middle more often than from lack of ability. Saving state periodically means not starting over.
durableExecution.heading: Durable Execution
durableExecution.note: Vibisual guarantees this layer in the core, so an agent never has to build its own resume path.

atomicWrite.desc: Dying mid-write leaves a half-written file, and the quiet corruption starts the moment the next boot reads it as valid. Writing to a temp file and swapping atomically is the standard.
atomicWrite.heading: Atomic Write
atomicWrite.note: The core writes its checkpoints and settings atomically with backup generations. Files the agent writes itself are not covered by that guarantee.

promptInjection.desc: Counts the paths through which outside text reaches this agent. The cause is structural — a model receives instructions and data on the same token stream and cannot tell them apart in principle.
promptInjection.heading: Prompt Injection
promptInjection.note: Every external text an agent reads is a potential path — search results, opened files, dependency READMEs, even what a tool returned.

owaspAsi.desc: Re-groups the earlier judgements along the agent-specific risk axes. What stands out is that more than half of those risks live in the harness rather than in the model — which is why this can be self-checked.
owaspAsi.heading: OWASP ASI Top 10
owaspAsi.note: Goal hijack, tool misuse, identity, memory poisoning and rogue agents are the items that come up most often in practice.

goalHijack.desc: Once the goal itself is swapped, every later step autonomously helps the attacker — and because the behaviour stays outwardly consistent, people rarely notice.
goalHijack.heading: Goal Hijack
goalHijack.note: Keep the goal somewhere it cannot be rewritten — do not put user instructions and tool results on the same layer.

memoryPoisoning.desc: Ordinary injection dies with the session; poisoned memory stays and infects future ones. Worse, it is trusted more because it looks like something the system learned.
memoryPoisoning.heading: Memory Poisoning
memoryPoisoning.note: Promotion into memory needs provenance — a fact from the user and a line read out of an external document must not be stored at the same trust level.

agenticSupplyChain.desc: Compromise arrives through what the agent depends on — malicious tools, untrusted servers, tampered skill files. A tool description is itself a prompt, so a hostile tool can hide instructions in it.
agenticSupplyChain.heading: Agentic Supply Chain
agenticSupplyChain.note: Treat an outside tool server as a delegation of authority, not a dependency — pin the source and version, and re-review on change.

cascadingFailure.desc: A wrong output becomes the next input and gets refined into something more confident at each step. Where a human team would ask “is this right?”, an agent takes it as a premise.
cascadingFailure.heading: Cascading Failure
cascadingFailure.note: Pass uncertainty across each boundary and keep a “could not confirm” field in the handoff. Self-feeding — an agent consuming its own signal — is the extreme form of this.

agentCard.desc: A machine-readable statement of what an agent can do. It only becomes usable for automatic selection once cost, latency and failure modes are written down too.
agentCard.heading: Agent Card
agentCard.note: Not every agent needs a full discovery stack — for simple setups a short instruction file is enough.

toolSearch.desc: Rather than loading every tool definition, search and load only the one needed. Calling a tool a hundred times piles a hundred intermediate results into the window; running it as code returns only the final one.
toolSearch.heading: Tool Search
toolSearch.note: The evolution of “use fewer tools” is “let it search for tools”. The bigger the catalogue, the larger the gain.

compactionWatch.desc: Folding past turns into a summary is the standard device for long work. Knowing where the loss happens is the skill — summaries drop concrete identifiers first.
compactionWatch.heading: Compaction Watch
compactionWatch.note: File paths, function names, error codes and the reasons behind decisions are exactly what a summary discards, and exactly what you need later.
compactionWatch.noteNear: The window is filling. Write the decisions and paths out to a file before automatic compaction runs.

contextEditing.desc: Instead of summarising, strip only old tool calls, results and thinking blocks by rule. It is the safest, least lossy form of compression — a finished tool result rarely needs to be seen again.
contextEditing.heading: Context Editing
contextEditing.note: Try this before compaction — it is cheaper and less risky, and server-side implementations no longer break the prompt cache prefix.

specDriven.desc: A versioned specification becomes the source of truth, and implementation, tests and docs derive from it. Once the spec removes ambiguity the agent works as a fast typist rather than a decision maker.
specDriven.heading: Spec-Driven Development
specDriven.note: This does not replace TDD — TDD pins behaviour, SDD pins requirements and constraints. They are used together.

preCommitGate.desc: Agents commit easily and often, and blocking before the fact is far cheaper than reviewing after. Secret leakage is the one category where after-the-fact response does not exist — once pushed, it is exposed.
preCommitGate.heading: Pre-commit Gate
preCommitGate.note: A gate the agent can bypass is not a gate. The minimum set is secret scanning, lint and typecheck, and blocked paths.

ssotDrift.desc: Counts how many places this agent takes direction from. When the same fact lives in two places they drift, and a model will cite both as if each were current.
ssotDrift.heading: SSOT Drift
ssotDrift.note: People skim past a stale line thinking “that is old”. Models quote it with confidence.

adrPresence.desc: Without a record of what was rejected and why, an agent will propose an already-discarded design in good faith. A decision record is where “do not do this” lives with its reason.
adrPresence.heading: Decision Records
adrPresence.note: Keeping decisions next to the code and referencing them from the instruction file is the standard layout.

schemaEvolution.desc: Add fields optionally with defaults and older saved state stays readable by newer code. Vibisual keeps checkpoints on that rule.
schemaEvolution.heading: Schema Evolution
schemaEvolution.note: Breaking backward compatibility means old checkpoints stop loading — which is exactly when a crash turns into lost work.

mcpClientInventory.desc: Counts external tool servers attached to this agent. One install line can bring in arbitrary code and tool definitions, so the list itself is worth inspecting.
mcpClientInventory.heading: MCP Inventory
mcpClientInventory.note: An untrusted server is a supply-chain risk, not a convenience. Pin source and version, and re-review on change.

a2a.desc: MCP connects an agent to the outside world; A2A is how agents work with each other. They are different layers, so “which one” is the wrong question.
a2a.heading: A2A
a2a.note: For subagents inside one process this protocol is overkill — its use is collaboration across organisational boundaries.

acpAnp.desc: The shared limitation of interoperability protocols is governance: they standardise what can connect to what, not who is allowed to do what.
acpAnp.heading: ACP and ANP
acpAnp.note: Adopting a protocol does not give you permission or audit design — those still have to be built separately.

agentsMd.desc: A single instruction file at the repository root became the de-facto standard, but longer is not better — past roughly 150 lines the returns drop sharply while inference cost keeps rising.
agentsMd.heading: Agent Instructions
agentsMd.note: Short instructions with links to detail is the right shape. Pasting whole documents in manufactures context rot.
agentsMd.noteLong: These rules are long enough to cost on every turn while the later parts get diluted first. Move detail out and link to it.

computerUse.desc: Driving software by looking at the screen reaches everything that has no API, but every step depends on visual grounding, which makes it slow and brittle.
computerUse.heading: Computer Use
computerUse.note: If it can be done through CLI or API, do not do it through the GUI. Irreversible clicks belong behind a human confirmation.

chunking.desc: Split too finely and context breaks; keep chunks too large and unrelated content rides along. In Vibisual one memory card is one chunk, so card size is the quality knob.
chunking.heading: Chunking
chunking.note: Because topics group the cards, chunk boundaries do not need separate tuning here — writing one idea per card does that job.

reranking.desc: First-pass retrieval casts wide; reranking lifts what is actually relevant. Vibisual injects only the top few cards, so that cap is the reranking result.
reranking.heading: Reranking
reranking.note: A tight cap is what keeps retrieval from turning into another source of context rot.

hybridSearch.desc: Keyword search is strong on exact names and paths; semantic search is strong when the wording differs. Vibisual searches memory on the keyword axis only, which is a deliberate choice at this scale.
hybridSearch.heading: Hybrid Search
hybridSearch.note: At a few hundred entries the second axis costs more to run than it returns. This card exists to notice when that stops being true.

multiHop.desc: Questions that one search cannot answer need a second query built on what the first one found. This counts how often the agent went back.
multiHop.heading: Multi-hop Retrieval
multiHop.note: Going back is a sign the agent noticed its evidence was incomplete — usually a good sign, not a wasted step.

queryRewriting.desc: The words a person uses and the words stored in knowledge rarely match, so the query has to be reshaped. Here the agent writes its own search terms, so rewriting happens on its side.
queryRewriting.heading: Query Rewriting
queryRewriting.note: Searches that keep coming back empty usually mean the stored wording and the asked wording never overlap.

benchmarkHygiene.desc: Public scores cluster at the top, test data leaks into training, and the same model scores differently under a different harness. Only a set built from your own domain is a trustworthy signal.
benchmarkHygiene.heading: Benchmark Hygiene
benchmarkHygiene.note: Lessons and check points recorded here are exactly the material an in-house evaluation set is built from.

hybridWorkflow.desc: Pure specification is slow and pure improvisation collapses, so where you draw the line is the skill. Interfaces, data models and permission boundaries call for a spec; the implementation inside can stay free.
hybridWorkflow.heading: Hybrid Workflow
hybridWorkflow.note: You can switch between the two within a single project as the phase changes — that is the point of the hybrid.

rescueEngineering.desc: Cleaning up quickly built code became a market of its own. The cost of speed did not vanish; it was deferred and comes back with interest.
rescueEngineering.heading: Rescue Engineering
rescueEngineering.note: Rule documents, evaluation sets, loss prevention and commit gates are all spending done up front — a fraction of what the rescue costs later.

promptCaching.desc: Reusing the same prefix on every request cuts cost and latency sharply, but the prefix has to match byte for byte — put a timestamp or a random id up front and the whole cache breaks.
promptCaching.heading: Prompt Caching
promptCaching.note: Hit rate lives in the provider response, so this card does not guess at it — it only checks whether the prefix is stable enough for caching to be possible. The rule is: changing things last, unchanging things first.

toolMisuse.desc: Scans the commands this agent actually ran for irreversible shapes. No intrusion is needed for misuse — the authority is already granted, which is why granting itself is part of the attack surface.
toolMisuse.heading: Tool Misuse
toolMisuse.note: Giving one shell tool and giving five named commands are completely different risk grades. Arguments need validation too, not just the tool list.
toolMisuse.noteFound: These already ran — this card reports, it does not block. The place that blocks is the approval prompt in front of the tool call.

dataExfiltration.desc: Looks for commands that send data outward. It does not inspect content — the point is whether an outbound path was actually used, because anything that left cannot be recalled.
dataExfiltration.heading: Data Exfiltration
dataExfiltration.note: What counts as “sending outward” is broad now — commits, pushes, API calls, image URL requests and webhooks all qualify.
dataExfiltration.noteUsed: Once content is out, deleting it later does not remove it from caches and indexes. Check what these commands carried.

mcpServer.desc: Shows whether Vibisual itself is exposed as a tool that outside clients can attach to. It is not — that exposure sits in the out-of-scope list, and this card exists so the decision stays visible.
mcpServer.heading: MCP Server
mcpServer.note: The side where we attach to outside servers is a different question and a different card. This one only reports our own exposure, and never turns it on.

killSwitch.desc: Adds a single control that stops everything running. It cancels scheduled loops first and then stops live sessions — killing only the current run leaves the scheduler to start the next one.
killSwitch.label: Stop all
killSwitch.title: Stop every running session and cancel scheduled loops ({{count}} agents)

agentRegistry.desc: Answers the practical question a registry exists for — who created this agent, what authority it holds, and when it last moved. If those cannot be answered, unregistered agents are simply running unseen.
agentRegistry.heading: Agent Registry
agentRegistry.note: Design the moment an agent is retired, not only the moment it is created — forced registration, expiring credentials and idle shutdown are operational discipline rather than security technology.
agentRegistry.noteExternal: This session was registered through hooks, so its lifecycle belongs to Claude Code. We can see it but we do not promote or retire it.

plugins.noMatch: Nothing matches that. Try a word from what you want it to do.

usage.badgeOnlyWhenNotable: The badge appears only when something is worth a look.
usage.readsConfigOnly: Nothing — it judges the settings alone.
usage.howToOff: Turn it on here. It takes effect immediately, no restart.
usage.howToOn: Already on. Open a bubble to see the card.

tabbar.confirmCloseMessage: A session is still running. Closing it will stop its work. Close anyway?

terminal.unavailable: The embedded terminal is available only in the Vibisual desktop app.
terminal.unavailableExternal: For security, the embedded terminal is disabled over external (internet) access — use it on your local network.
terminal.harnessNote: Interactive session you drive — Vibisual visualizes & assists harness wiring, but execution authority lives inside Claude Code.

taskEdgePopup.templateTooltip: Select a preset pair. Picking one auto-fills Type, Gate, and all advanced options below.
taskEdgePopup.templateSelect: Preset role pair. Selecting one prefills the whole form with sensible defaults.
taskEdgePopup.messageTooltip: The instruction sent to the target agent. Press Ctrl/Cmd+Enter to submit.
taskEdgePopup.typeTooltip: What this edge means — Command (instruction), Artifact (deliverable), Request (help ask), Critique (review). Edge color reflects this in the map.
taskEdgePopup.gateTooltip: Auto: runs as soon as saved. Manual: requires a human to press Run. Use Manual for anything destructive or high-impact.
taskEdgePopup.autoTooltip: Auto: executes immediately when the edge is saved. Fastest, but skips human review.
taskEdgePopup.manualTooltip: Manual: waits for a human to press Run. Safer for destructive or high-impact tasks.
taskEdgePopup.advancedTooltip: Message format / Return format / Timeout / Retry / Cache / Priority. Templates prefill these with sensible defaults — usually no change needed. (Execution logic is a future step; this version only stores the values.)
taskEdgePopup.advancedShow: Show advanced options: message format, return format, timeout, retry, cache, priority.
taskEdgePopup.messageFormatTooltip: Free: easy but ambiguous. Schema: key/value, structured. Prefer Schema for critical or repeatable tasks.
taskEdgePopup.freeTextTooltip: Free text: natural-language instruction. Fast to write, but the AI may misread nuance.
taskEdgePopup.schemaTooltip: Schema: structured key/value input. More upfront work, fewer downstream surprises.
taskEdgePopup.schemaEditTooltip: Open the schema editor. Type the format the source agent should follow when sending through this edge.
taskEdgePopup.schemaEditHint: Free-form text. The source agent will be told to format its outbound message in this shape. Leave empty to send as plain text.
taskEdgePopup.schemaPlaceholder:
Example:
{
  "goal": "...",
  "context": "...",
  "acceptance": ["..."]
}

— or natural-language —
Reply with: 1) what you changed, 2) which files, 3) any open risks.
taskEdgePopup.returnFormatTooltip: Artifact: actual file/diff paths. Summary: text summary only. Both: both. AI summaries can be wrong; prefer Artifact for anything you need to verify.
taskEdgePopup.artifactTooltip: Artifact: return the actual file path or diff. Verifiable by you.
taskEdgePopup.summaryTooltip: Summary: short text summary only. Fast, but AI summaries can be inaccurate.
taskEdgePopup.bothTooltip: Both: return the artifact and a summary so you can scan before diving in.
taskEdgePopup.timeoutTooltip: Max run duration in milliseconds. Leave blank for unlimited. Example: 60000 = 1 minute. Guards against runaway loops.
taskEdgePopup.retryTooltip: How many times to retry on failure. 0 = no retries. Useful for transient failures like network hiccups.
taskEdgePopup.retryDisabledNote: Coming soon — retry logic is not implemented yet. Value is saved as metadata only.
taskEdgePopup.priorityTooltip: Run order when multiple edges are ready. High runs first. Default Normal.
taskEdgePopup.priorityDisabledNote: Coming soon — priority scheduling is not implemented yet. Value is saved as metadata only.
taskEdgePopup.priorityLowTooltip: Low: runs only when nothing else is queued.
taskEdgePopup.priorityHighTooltip: High: jumps ahead of other pending edges.
taskEdgePopup.cacheTooltip: Reuse the previous result when inputs match (saves tokens). Turn OFF if the underlying data changes often.
taskEdgePopup.cacheLabelTooltip: When the input matches a previous run, reuse that result instead of re-running. Saves tokens. Turn OFF if underlying data changes often.
taskEdgePopup.cacheDisabledNote: Coming soon — result cache is not implemented yet. Value is saved as metadata only.
taskEdgePopup.delegationTooltip: STRICT: tasks matching this edge's purpose must be delegated through it. The source agent cannot handle them with its own Read/Grep. AUTO: the source agent decides whether to delegate based on cost and fit (3+ exploration steps / purpose match / target suitability). Simple 1-2 Read calls stay in-agent.
taskEdgePopup.delegationStrictTooltip: Mandatory delegation when the edge purpose matches. No self-handling. (Default)
taskEdgePopup.delegationAutoTooltip: The source agent decides autonomously based on exploration cost and fit.
taskEdgePopup.commandOptionsTooltip: Command-edge specifics (kind='command' only). Orthogonal to Delegation Policy: this controls the FORM of delegation, not whether it's enforced.
taskEdgePopup.commandModeTooltip: How tools are shared between parent and child. Shared: parent keeps every tool, can call directly or delegate. Tool delegation: tools the child has are stripped from the parent — delegation enforced naturally. Mode delegation: tools stay shared but the parent is instructed to delegate operations whose mode (plan / acceptEdits / specific model / skill) is the child's specialty.
taskEdgePopup.commandModeSharedTooltip: Parent keeps the tools. Both parent and child can run them. Delegation is recommended via prompt only. (Default — safest.)
taskEdgePopup.commandModeToolTooltip: Tools the child agent has are removed from the parent. The parent must dispatch via this edge to use them. (= Pre-v1.44 strict behavior.)
taskEdgePopup.commandModeModeTooltip: Parent keeps the tools, but the system prompt forces delegation of operations whose mode (plan / acceptEdits / specific model / skill) is the child's specialty. Pseudo-tool injection is a future round.
taskEdgePopup.commandModeModeNote: Mode delegation does not strip any tools — the parent is told via system prompt to delegate operations matching the child's mode. PreToolUse hook gating is planned for a follow-up.
taskEdgePopup.commandStripPreviewTooltip: Live computed: child agent's tools ∩ parent agent's tools. These are the tools the parent will lose access to when this edge is active.
taskEdgePopup.commandStripPreviewEmpty: No overlap — parent and child share no tools. Strip would be a no-op. Consider Mode delegation instead.
taskEdgePopup.cancelTooltip: Discard changes and close. The live preview on the canvas will revert.
taskEdgePopup.saveTooltip: Save these changes to the edge (Ctrl/Cmd+Enter).
taskEdgePopup.connectTooltip: Create the edge with these settings (Ctrl/Cmd+Enter).
taskEdgePopup.critiqueOptionsTip: Critique-edge only. Sets when to intervene (Timing) and what to enforce on reject (Authority). Ignored for other kinds.
taskEdgePopup.critiqueTimingTip: Intermediate (default): review at each milestone during the target's work. More frequent / safer / slower. Final: a single final review after completion. Less frequent / faster.
taskEdgePopup.critiqueTimingIntermediateTip: Intermediate: review at each milestone during the target's work. (default)
taskEdgePopup.critiqueTimingFinalTip: Final only: a single final review after the target completes.
taskEdgePopup.critiqueAuthorityTip: Force rework (default): on reject the target must redo the work. Exceeding Max Rework auto-downgrades to comment-only and escalates to the parent session. Comment only: reject is advisory only, no forced rework.
taskEdgePopup.critiqueAuthorityForceTip: Force rework: the target must redo on reject. (default)
taskEdgePopup.critiqueAuthorityCommentTip: Comment only: the target only takes the reject as a reference. No forced rework.
taskEdgePopup.critiqueMaxReworkTip: Max times the target may redo while in Force rework mode. Exceeding it auto-downgrades to comment-only and escalates to the parent session. A guard against infinite loops.
taskEdgePopup.critiqueMaxReworkActive: Max {{max}} times. Auto-downgrades to comment-only when exceeded.
taskEdgePopup.critiqueMaxReworkInactive: Not used in Comment only mode.
